title: bank-aware-memory-pacing-kv-eviction-experiments
content:
Summary:

Quick notes from a set of microbench tests exploring whether pacing memory access on a per-memory-bank basis can reduce KV cache eviction-induced paging and tail latencies for mixed-seqlen workloads. This doc captures hypothesis, bench setup, observations, and next steps. Intended as a working log for the runtime team; rough data and graphs referenced inline are in the linked PR and the lab spreadsheet.

Background / motivation:
- We see long-tail token latencies and periodic spike in page-fault counts when mixed short/long requests ride the same KV cache.
- Previous probes showed that contention often correlates to one or two memory channels (banks) being hot and saturating DMA lanes, triggering spillback and aggressive eviction on neighboring pages.
- Hypothesis: If we can smooth per-bank bandwidth usage using a light-weight pacing layer (throttle requests that would create large bursts to a single bank), we can spread pressure, reduce paging, and improve P95/P99 without a large throughput penalty.

Hypothesis details:
- Hot-spot behavior arises from long-seq requests that polarize attention lookups to a subset of KV pages (token embedding caches aligned to model layers).
- These lookups generate bursts that exceed per-bank DMA throughput; the OS/hw then serializes transfers, causing stalls and working-set eviction on other banks.
- A simple token-level pacing (delay a few microseconds for requests that would hit the same bank back-to-back) should reduce short-term burstiness and give the background evictor/prefetcher time to coalesce transfers.

Testbed and harness:
- Machine: 8x A100-like GPU host, 6-channel DDRx config (representative of our private clusters).
- Runtime: local dev branch bank-pacing-experiments (PR: linked). Build: debug-with-profiling flags to capture hw counters.
- Workloads: synthetic mix of 60% short (seqlen 32) chat-style requests and 40% long (seqlen 2048) streaming requests. Arrival process: Poisson with variable burst factor.
- KV config: 24GB KV partition per model, page size 2MB, LRU-based eviction.
- Telemetry captured: per-bank DMA bytes/sec, page-faults/sec (kernel), kv-eviction-rate, p50/p95/p99 token latency, throughput (requests/sec).
- Commands / bench harness snippet: make bench && ./bench_driver --workload mixed_seqlen --burst 3 --concurrency 64 --duration 30m --profile bank_counters.csv

Pacing implementation (prototype):
- Lock-free counters per-bank updated by lookup path; when a lookup would push a bank's counter over threshold (X MB in last Y us), the request yields for t microseconds (configurable).
- Thresholds tuned empirically: X = 12 MB in Y = 200 us; t ranges 50-400 us depending on dynamic mode.
- Fallback: if global throughput drops below 90% of baseline, reduce t by 50% to avoid throughput collapse.

Key results (representative runs):
- Baseline (no pacing):
  - page-faults: 9.8 / sec
  - kv-evictions: 280 / min
  - p99 token latency: 230 ms
  - throughput: 820 req/s
- Bank-pacing (static t=200us):
  - page-faults: 5.6 / sec (−43%)
  - kv-evictions: 190 / min (−32%)
  - p99 token latency: 160 ms (−30%)
  - throughput: 790 req/s (−3.7%)
- Bank-pacing (adaptive):
  - page-faults: 4.4 / sec (−55%)
  - kv-evictions: 165 / min (−41%)
  - p99 token latency: 140 ms (−39%)
  - throughput: 770 req/s (−6.1%)

Observations and interpretation:
- Per-bank counters correlate strongly with observed page-fault spikes. When a bank exceeds ~10–14 MB in a few hundred microseconds, a burst of page faults and eviction events follows within 1–4 ms.
- Pacing reduces instantaneous DMA peaks and gives the OS hardware prefetch/merge logic time to coalesce transfers; that reduces page-fault amplification.
- The throughput penalty is modest for mixed workloads, but sensitive to workload composition. Pure-short or pure-long workloads show near-zero benefit and unnecessary pacing overhead; therefore adaptive enabling is critical.
- We saw cases where naive static pacing increased average latency for pure-short workloads; adaptive mode prevented that by toggling pacing when the hot-bank count is low.

Telemetry traces (where to find them):
- bank_counters.csv attached to PR 842 contains per-run counters.
- lab sheet: https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/EXPERIMENTS_BANK_PACING (internal) with full runs and per-channel plots.

Failure modes and caveats:
- Host NIC/PCIe traffic can interact badly with bank pacing; if other co-scheduled jobs push the same memory channels, our pacing makes little difference. Must test on isolated nodes for reliable measurements.
- Hardware with internal cross-channel balancing may not benefit as much; this change seems most helpful on boards with weak hardware balancing.
- Pacing introduces jitter; some latency-sensitive tails improved via fewer page faults, but average latency can increase slightly in some mixes. Must be controlled.

Actionable next steps:
1) Expand test matrix: try additional seqlen mixes (10/90, 80/20) and vary batch sizes across ranges 1–128.
2) Run on two more hardware configs (8-channel DDR and 4-channel host) to see sensitivity to bank count.
3) Add feature flag in runtime for adaptive bank-aware pacing (default off). Include telemetry to track percent time throttled per request.
4) Build canary for dedicated pool (low-traffic) to validate in production-like environment before enabling more broadly.

Short-term implementation checklist:
- [ ] Merge prototype PR with metric emissions (PR 842).
- [ ] Add unit tests for counter correctness under concurrency.
- [ ] Create a toggleable runtime flag and conf.yaml knobs (threshold, sample-window, max-yield-us).
- [ ] Dashboard: per-bank DMA, throttle-time, page-fault delta.

Open questions / discussion items:
- What is an acceptable throughput headroom to trade for tail latency improvements for Hosted API customers? (should be configurable per-customer tier)
- Can we leverage hardware performance counters directly instead of software counters to reduce overhead? (need kernel/module/permission conversation)
- Should pacing be applied only when eviction pressure exceeds a threshold (e.g., measured resident set churn), rather than purely bank-peak driven?

Notes to self / rough TODOs:
- Save run id mapping to lab sheet for quick lookup: run-20241105-bankpacing-01..05
- Coordinate with SRE to run isolated cluster jobs next week (request through infra tickets).

References:
- PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/842
- JIRA: JIRA-RT-1174 (bank-aware pacing prototype)
